Before a public push, inspect git status, review the staged diff, and scan files for likely secrets. A text search is only a screening aid; it cannot prove that a repository is safe to publish.

Clone, update, and contribute through review

For a first-time checkout, run the first two commands once. On later visits, skip them and start in the existing repository directory. Before updating it, check that the working tree is clean. If git status --short lists changes, inspect and preserve them before switching branches. This example assumes the shared default branch is named main:

git clone https://github.com/OWNER/REPOSITORY.git
cd REPOSITORY

# Before updating an existing clean clone, run these commands from its directory.
git status --short
# Continue only if this prints nothing.
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main

To propose a small change, start from the updated main branch, work on a topic branch, inspect the diff, and push that branch rather than committing directly to main:

git switch -c docs/input-notes
# Edit README.md in your editor, then inspect the change before staging.
git diff --check
git diff -- README.md
git add README.md
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Clarify project input notes"
git push -u origin docs/input-notes

Open a pull request with main as the base. A reviewer should check the complete diff, test results, and data permissions before approval and merge. If you do not have write access, fork the repository, clone your fork, and propose the change back to the original repository. After a pull request is merged, update a clean local main branch with the fast-forward-only commands above; for a fork, configure the original repository as upstream and use that remote in place of origin. If a fast-forward is not possible, stop and inspect both histories rather than using a force push or hard reset. Follow the repository's review policy and never include sensitive data.

Read the repository state

  • git status reports staged, modified, and untracked paths. A clean working tree means no uncommitted changes are visible to Git; it does not mean every required file is tracked.

Interpreting clone-associated expression

A clone-size category is an abundance grouping, not a malignancy label. In a lymphoma study, determining whether a clone is malignant requires disease-specific evidence and study design beyond this repertoire workflow. A cell-level contrast such as FindMarkers() can be exploratory, but cells from the same donor are not independent biological replicates. For condition-level claims, account for between-sample variation, for example with an appropriate pseudobulk design, and validate findings independently.

TCRs and BCRs share V(D)J-based diversity but differ in chain organization and biology. The main code above is TCR-focused. For a real BCR analysis, use BCR-specific handling such as combineBCR() on filtered contig annotations and verify productive IGH plus IGK and/or IGL chains and CDR3 fields. For combineExpression(), choose a BCR-appropriate clone.call and chain (documented choices include IGH, IGL, and both); the scRepertoire documentation describes its heavy/light-chain handling and related-clone options. A heavy-chain-only call does not represent paired receptors. Check barcode overlap and resulting metadata before plotting. Interpret pairing and somatic hypermutation with BCR-specific methods. The small synthetic example below is a teaching summary, not a validated BCR pipeline.

BCR: reproducible synthetic example

This base R exercise starts from invented, normalized contig rows with one row per chain call. It needs no external data or packages. It checks whether each barcode has a productive heavy chain and at least one productive light chain, then counts distinct cells by an explicitly simplified exact heavy-chain key: sample, V gene, J gene, and CDR3 amino-acid sequence. This key is not a scRepertoire clone call and may split related sequences that differ through somatic hypermutation.

bcr <- data.frame(
  sample_id = rep("toy_A", 8),
  cell_barcode = c("cell_01", "cell_01", "cell_02", "cell_02",
                   "cell_03", "cell_03", "cell_04", "cell_04"),
  chain = c("IGH", "IGK", "IGH", "IGK", "IGH", "IGL", "IGH", "IGK"),
  productive = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE),
  v_gene = c("IGHV1-2", NA_character_, "IGHV1-2", NA_character_,
             "IGHV3-7", NA_character_, "IGHV1-2", NA_character_),
  j_gene = c("IGHJ4", NA_character_, "IGHJ4", NA_character_,
             "IGHJ6", NA_character_, "IGHJ4", NA_character_),
  junction_aa = c("CARGGYYGMDV", NA_character_, "CARGGYYGMDV", NA_character_,
                  "CARRDYGMDV", NA_character_, "CARGGYYGMDV", NA_character_),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

productive_bcr <- subset(bcr, productive)
chains_by_cell <- split(
  productive_bcr$chain,
  paste(productive_bcr$sample_id, productive_bcr$cell_barcode, sep = ":")
)
has_paired_chains <- vapply(chains_by_cell, function(chains) {
  "IGH" %in% chains && any(chains %in% c("IGK", "IGL"))
}, logical(1))
stopifnot(sum(has_paired_chains) == 3L, sum(!has_paired_chains) == 1L)
cat("cells_with_IGH_and_light=", sum(has_paired_chains),
    "; without_productive_pair=", sum(!has_paired_chains), "\n", sep = "")

productive_igh <- subset(productive_bcr, chain == "IGH")
bcr_clones <- aggregate(
  cell_barcode ~ sample_id + v_gene + j_gene + junction_aa,
  data = productive_igh,
  FUN = function(x) length(unique(x))
)
names(bcr_clones)[names(bcr_clones) == "cell_barcode"] <- "cells"
bcr_clones <- bcr_clones[order(-bcr_clones$cells, bcr_clones$junction_aa), ]
stopifnot(identical(as.integer(bcr_clones$cells), c(2L, 1L)))
write.table(bcr_clones, row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE, sep = "\t")

Expected output (tab-separated after the first line):

cells_with_IGH_and_light=3; without_productive_pair=1
sample_id	v_gene	j_gene	junction_aa	cells
toy_A	IGHV1-2	IGHJ4	CARGGYYGMDV	2
toy_A	IGHV3-7	IGHJ6	CARRDYGMDV	1

In this toy table, three cells have a productive IGH and at least one productive IGK or IGL; one has only productive IGK after its nonproductive IGH row is excluded. The summary counts invented cell barcodes only. Real data can contain multiple productive contigs, doublets, or barcode mismatches, so inspect chain multiplicity and sample-aware barcode handling before calling paired receptors or interpreting counts. This exact amino-acid grouping does not infer lineage, affinity, antigen specificity, or biological function. For BCR clone calling and somatic-hypermutation analysis, use a version-appropriate BCR method and report its parameters.

Decisions to report with your analysis

  • Input and denominator: assay/software output, included samples, and whether abundance counts cells or another unit.
